# Fundamentals and State of the Art {#sec-fundamentals}

This chapter explains the background that is needed to follow the rest of the thesis.
It starts with the application, the lighting of an aircraft cabin
(@sec-cabin-lighting). It then explains how LEDs work and how their brightness is controlled (@sec-led-dimming), how an FPGA is built (@sec-fpga-fundamentals) and how a design is brought onto an FPGA (@sec-design-flow). The last technical parts describe serial communication (@sec-serial-communication) and the Flexlink protocol (@sec-flexlink). The chapter ends with an overview of existing solutions and the research gap that this thesis addresses (@sec-state-of-the-art).

## Aircraft Cabin Lighting {#sec-cabin-lighting}

Previously, the lighting system used for aircraft cabins came from **fluorescent technology**, and LEDs were first added only for *coloured mood lighting*. As the efficiency of LEDs increased, they became able to produce the **white light** as well [@krellera2009]. Currently, aircrafts such as the **Airbus A380** and the **Boeing 787** use LED cabin lighting systems that combine white light and coloured LEDs [@lumileds2015].

Light Emitting Diodes offers several advantages that are vital in an aircraft when compared to older light sources. A supplier of such systems reports energy savings of **35 % to 55 %** compared with previous lighting systems, and a lifetime of about **50,000 hours**, which is roughly ten times longer than that of incandescent, fluorescent or halogen lamps. Because LEDs are solid-state devices, they are also smaller, lighter and more resistant to vibration and shock, which reduces fuel consumption and maintenance [@lumileds2015].

The colour control of LEDs allows the cabin light changes with the phase of the flight which is known as *light scenes*. For instance, bright light for boarding, settings that imitate a sunrise in the morning, and a cool light in the evening. On long flights, such programmes are used to shift the sleep rhythm of the passengers slowly towards the time zone of the destination [@lumileds2015]. The aim is to support the mood and the biorhythm of the
passengers and to create a pleasant atmosphere [@krellera2009].

Electronic equipment for aircraft must meet strict rules. In the European Union, the **European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA)** is responsible for the certification of
aircraft and their equipment. For the technical details, EASA and the U.S authorities
rely on industry standards that are published jointly by **EUROCAE** in Europe and **RTCA** in
the USA. EUROCAE ED-14G, which is identically worded to RTCA DO-160G, defines
environmental test conditions for airborne equipment, for example *temperature, vibration and electromagnetic compatibility* [@eurocae_ed14g]. EUROCAE ED-80, which
corresponds to RTCA DO-254, gives design assurance guidance for airborne electronic
hardware, including complex programmable devices such as FPGAs. EASA recognises this
standard in its Acceptable Means of Compliance *AMC 20-152A* [@easa_amc20152a].
Certification according to these documents is outside the scope of this thesis
(@sec-scope), but they explain why reliability, simple and traceable design, and
documented verification are important for any design that is meant for an aircraft.

## LEDs and LED Dimming {#sec-led-dimming}

### LED Basics {#sec-led-basics}

An **LED** is a semiconductor diode that emits light when a current flows through it in the
forward direction. The voltage across the LED in this state is called the **forward voltage** $V_F$. It
depends on the semiconductor material and therefore on the colour. For a typical *5 mm LED* family, the forward voltage at *20 mA* is about **2.1 V** for a red LED (AlInGaP) and
about **3.2 V** for green and blue LEDs (InGaN) [@avago_hlmp_hx64]. In general, standard
red, green and yellow LEDs have forward voltages of **1.4 V to 2.6 V**, while blue and white
LEDs need about **3.1 V to 4.0 V**, depending on the manufacturer [@maxim2004].

The datasheet of a typical 5 mm LED family shows this effect clearly that the dominant
wavelength of a green InGaN LED changes by several nanometres when the forward current
changes between low values and 100 mA [@avago_hlmp_hx64].

@fig-led-iv shows the typical shape of the current-voltage curve. Below the forward
voltage, almost no current flows. Above it, the current rises very steeply, so a small
change of the voltage gives a large change of the current. For this reason, an LED is
always operated with a resistor or a current source that limits the current.

![Current-voltage curves of a red and a green/blue LED, drawn with a simple diode model. The points mark the typical forward voltages at 20 mA [@avago_hlmp_hx64].](images/ch2_led_iv_curve){#fig-led-iv width=80%}

### RGBW Colour Mixing {#sec-rgbw}

Each LED has one fixed color when it emits light in a narrow range of wavelengths. In a typical 5 mm LED family, for example, the red LED has a *dominant wavelength*
of 626 nm, the green LED 525 nm and the blue LED 470 nm [@avago_hlmp_hx64].
The light of several LEDs is mixed in order to produce other colors, which are called *primaries* [@doe_ledcolor2012].When a red, a green and a blue LED (**RGB**) light up the same area, the eye sees one
mixed colour, which depends on how bright each LED is compared with the other two
(@fig-colour-mixing).

![Mixing the light of red, green and blue LEDs.](images/ch2_colour_mixing){#fig-colour-mixing width=60%}

White light can also be produced in this way, by mixing red, green and blue. In general
lighting, however, white LEDs are mostly made by *phosphor conversion*: a blue or
near-ultraviolet LED chip is combined with a phosphor that emits yellow light
[@doe_ledcolor2012]. Compared with such phosphor-converted white LEDs, mixed RGB systems
have a lower *efficacy* and less colour consistency, both at the start and over time,
because the red, green and blue LEDs lose brightness at different rates as they age
[@doe_ledcolor2012]. A fourth, white LED is therefore often added to the three coloured
ones (**RGBW**). The white LED provides the white light directly, while the coloured LEDs
are used to set the colour. The LED cabin lighting of aircraft such as the Boeing 787 and
the Airbus A380 also uses a combination of white and coloured LEDs [@lumileds2015].

The colour of white light is described by its **correlated colour temperature (CCT)**,
which is given in kelvin (K). It is the temperature at which a heated *black body* would
have the colour that is closest to the colour of the light source. The CCT describes how
"warm" (yellowish) or how "cool" (bluish) a white light appears [@doe_ledcolor2012]. A
lower CCT appears warmer, a higher CCT cooler. Changing the CCT is part of the light
scenes in a cabin, for example a light that imitates a sunrise in the morning and a cooler
light in the evening [@lumileds2015]. With RGBW, such changes are made by changing the
brightness of the four channels.

For the control electronics, RGBW means four separate channels per segment, one for
each colour. The brightness of every channel must be set on its own. With a resolution
of 16 bit, each channel has

$$
2^{16} = 65{,}536
$$ {#eq-16bit-steps}

brightness steps, from 0 (off) to 65,535 (full brightness).

The same brightness value does **not** give the same light output for every colour. At
the same current of 20 mA, the *luminous intensity* given in the datasheet of the LED
family mentioned above is 1150 mcd to 2400 mcd for the red LED, 1990 mcd to 5040 mcd for
the green LED and 460 mcd to 1150 mcd for the blue LED [@avago_hlmp_hx64]. A green LED can
therefore appear several times brighter than a blue LED at the same current. To produce a
wanted colour, each channel needs its own brightness value. In this thesis, the node only
applies the brightness values it receives from the master (@sec-flexlink).

### Analog Dimming vs. PWM Dimming {#sec-analog-vs-pwm}

There are two basic ways to change the brightness of an LED:

1. *Analog dimming*: the DC current through the LED is reduced.
2. *Pulse-width modulation (PWM) dimming*: the LED is switched fully on and fully off
   many times per second. The current is either zero or at its set value, and the
   brightness depends on how long the LED is on in each period.

Analog dimming is the simpler method, but changing the LED current also changes the
*chromaticity* of the LED, so its colour shifts. With PWM dimming, the current is either
off or at its set level, so the chromaticity stays the same [@parasseril2006]. The
datasheet of the 5 mm LED family used as an example above shows this effect: the
dominant wavelength of the green LED changes by up to about 10 nm when the forward
current changes between low values and 100 mA, and the blue LED shows a smaller but
similar shift [@avago_hlmp_hx64]. In an RGBW system, a colour shift in one channel
changes the mixed colour. **PWM dimming is therefore used when the colour has to stay
exact.** @tbl-dimming-methods compares the two methods.

| **Property**             | **Analog dimming**                   | **PWM dimming**                          |
|:-------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| How brightness is set    | size of the DC current               | ratio of on-time to period               |
| Colour stability         | colour shifts with current           | colour stays the same                    |
| Circuit                  | adjustable current source            | switch and digital timing                |
| Possible problem         | colour shift                         | flicker if the frequency is too low      |

: Comparison of analog and PWM dimming, based on [@parasseril2006; @avago_hlmp_hx64] {#tbl-dimming-methods}

### PWM Parameters and Flicker {#sec-pwm-parameters}

A PWM signal is a square wave with a fixed period $T$. In each period, the signal is high
for the time $t_\text{on}$ and low for the rest of the period. The *duty cycle* $D$ is the
part of the period in which the signal is high:

$$
D = \frac{t_\text{on}}{T}
$$ {#eq-duty-cycle}

If the LED current during the on-time is $I_\text{LED}$, the average current, and with it
the perceived brightness, is:

$$
I_\text{avg} = D \cdot I_\text{LED}
$$ {#eq-avg-current}

For example, with $I_\text{LED} = 20\ \text{mA}$ and $D = 25\ \%$, the average current is
$I_\text{avg} = 0.25 \cdot 20\ \text{mA} = 5\ \text{mA}$.

@fig-pwm-duty shows two PWM signals with duty cycles of 25 % and 75 %
![Ideal PWM signals with 25 % and 75 % duty cycle at $f_\text{PWM} \approx 763$ Hz.](images/ch2_pwm_duty_cycle){#fig-pwm-duty width=90%}

In a digital circuit, a PWM signal is usually made with a *counter* and a *comparator*.
The counter counts clock cycles from $0$ to $2^N - 1$ and then starts again, where $N$ is
the resolution in bits. The output is high while the counter value is smaller than the
brightness value. With this simple rule, the largest value $2^N - 1$ would still leave
the output low for one clock cycle in every period. The design in this thesis therefore
treats the largest value as "always on" (@sec-rtl). One full count is one PWM period, so
the PWM frequency is:

$$
f_\text{PWM} = \frac{f_\text{clk}}{2^N}
$$ {#eq-pwm-frequency}

With the values used in this thesis, $f_\text{clk} = 50\ \text{MHz}$ and $N = 16$:

1. Number of steps: $2^{16} = 65{,}536$.
2. PWM frequency: $f_\text{PWM} = 50{,}000{,}000\ \text{Hz} / 65{,}536 \approx 762.9\ \text{Hz}$.
3. PWM period: $T = 65{,}536 / 50{,}000{,}000\ \text{Hz} \approx 1.31\ \text{ms}$.
4. Smallest step, one clock cycle: $1 / 50\ \text{MHz} = 20\ \text{ns}$.

@eq-pwm-frequency shows the basic trade-off of digital PWM: for a fixed clock, every
additional bit of resolution halves the PWM frequency.

Because the light of a PWM-dimmed LED is switched on and off, the light output changes
over time. If this change is slow enough, people can see it as *flicker*, or it can lead
to other effects such as stroboscopic effects. A common measure is the *percent flicker*:

$$
\text{Percent flicker} = 100\ \% \cdot \frac{L_\text{max} - L_\text{min}}{L_\text{max} + L_\text{min}}
$$ {#eq-percent-flicker}

where $L_\text{max}$ and $L_\text{min}$ are the highest and the lowest light output within
one period. For a PWM signal that switches the LED fully off, $L_\text{min} = 0$, so the
percent flicker is $100\ \%$ for every duty cycle below $100\ \%$.

The recommended practice IEEE 1789-2015 gives limits for flicker in LED lighting. Miller
and Lehman explain how to apply it in a presentation for the Solid-State Lighting program
of the U.S. Department of Energy. Lehman was the chair of the IEEE working group that wrote
the recommended practice. For a flicker frequency of at least 100 Hz, the highest allowed
percent flicker is the frequency multiplied by $0.08$. A product that stays below this
value is acceptable for all but the most unusually sensitive persons, and at 1250 Hz or
higher, 100 % flicker is allowed [@miller_lehman2015].

For the PWM frequency of this thesis:

1. Low-risk limit at 762.9 Hz: $0.08 \cdot 762.9 \approx 61\ \%$.
2. Percent flicker of full on-off PWM: $100\ \%$.
3. Since $100\ \% > 61\ \%$, a full on-off PWM at 762.9 Hz is above the low-risk level of
   IEEE 1789, although it meets the AES requirement of more than 400 Hz.

This point is discussed again in the evaluation (@sec-evaluation).

### Low-Side Switching with a Transistor {#sec-low-side-switching}

An FPGA output cannot drive a typical LED directly. Its current is limited, and its
voltage can be lower than the forward voltage of the LED. The blue and green LEDs of the
5 mm family mentioned above, for example, have a typical forward voltage of 3.2 V at
20 mA [@avago_hlmp_hx64], which is higher than the output level of about 2.5 V of the
evaluation board used in this thesis (@sec-gatemate-board). A transistor is therefore
used as a switch between the FPGA and the LED.

In a *low-side switch*, the transistor sits between the LED and ground. The LED and its
series resistor are connected to the supply voltage $V_S$, and the transistor opens or
closes the path to ground. The LED then gets its power from $V_S$, and the FPGA only has
to drive the control input of the transistor.

![Low-side switch of one LED channel as used in the prototype. The FPGA output drives the gate of the BS170 through 100 Ω, and 10 kΩ keeps the gate at 0 V while the FPGA is not configured.](images/ch2_low_side_switch){#fig-low-side width=55%}

When the transistor is on, the series resistor sets the LED current. The resistor that
gives the wanted current $I_\text{LED}$ is:

$$
R = \frac{V_S - V_F - V_\text{sw}}{I_\text{LED}}
$$ {#eq-series-resistor}

where $V_F$ is the forward voltage of the LED and $V_\text{sw}$ is the voltage across the
switched-on transistor. The prototype uses an N-channel *MOSFET* as the switch
(@fig-low-side).

A MOSFET is controlled by its gate-source voltage $V_{GS}$. The gate is isolated from the
channel, so it draws no steady current, and the control circuit only has to charge the
small gate capacitance at each edge. The *threshold voltage* $V_{GS(th)}$ is the gate
voltage at which a small drain current, commonly 1 mA, starts to flow
[@nexperia_an90001]. At this voltage the MOSFET has only started to turn on. It reaches its
low on-resistance $R_{DS(\text{on})}$ only when it is *fully enhanced*, which needs about
5 V for logic-level MOSFETs and about 10 V for standard-level MOSFETs. A MOSFET that is only
partly on works in its linear region and turns a large part of the power into heat
[@nexperia_an90001]. In the on-state, its power loss is:

$$
P_\text{cond} = I_\text{LED}^2 \cdot R_{DS(\text{on})}
$$ {#eq-conduction-loss}

The MOSFET used in this thesis is the **BS170**. It can switch up to 500 mA at up to 60 V,
and its gate capacitance is at most 60 pF. Its threshold voltage lies between 0.8 V and
3.0 V, with a typical value of 2.0 V, and its on-resistance is specified only for a gate
voltage of 10 V [@onsemi_bs170]. With a gate drive of only about 2.5 V from the evaluation
board, a typical BS170 is switched on, but **not fully enhanced**. For small LED currents
this is enough, but it is not guaranteed by the datasheet for every part.

Example with typical values, to show how the series resistor is sized (the values of the
prototype follow in @sec-hw-driver):

1. LED: blue, $V_F = 3.2\ \text{V}$ at $I_\text{LED} = 20\ \text{mA}$ [@avago_hlmp_hx64].
2. Supply voltage $V_S = 12\ \text{V}$, assumed voltage across the switched-on MOSFET
   $V_\text{sw} = 0.2\ \text{V}$.
3. Series resistor: $R = (12 - 3.2 - 0.2)\ \text{V} / 0.02\ \text{A} = 8.6\ \text{V} / 0.02\ \text{A} = 430\ \Omega$.
4. Power in the resistor: $P_R = I^2 R = (0.02\ \text{A})^2 \cdot 430\ \Omega \approx 0.17\ \text{W}$,
   so a 0.25 W resistor is enough.

## FPGA Fundamentals {#sec-fpga-fundamentals}

### FPGA Architecture {#sec-fpga-architecture}

A **field-programmable gate array (FPGA)** is an integrated circuit that contains many
small programmable logic blocks, a programmable network of wires between them, and
programmable input/output (I/O) blocks around the edge of the chip [@kuon2008]. The user
decides what each logic block does and how the blocks are connected by loading a
configuration file, the *bitstream*. The same chip can therefore implement very
different digital circuits.

The basic logic block contains a *look-up table* (LUT) and a *flip-flop*. A LUT with $k$
inputs is a small memory with $2^k$ entries. By filling this memory, the LUT can produce
any logic function of its $k$ inputs. The flip-flop stores one bit and takes over a new
value at each clock edge, which allows counters, shift registers and other sequential
circuits [@kuon2008]. Besides these blocks, modern FPGAs contain special blocks such as
*block RAM* for storing data and *phase-locked loops* (PLLs) for generating clock signals
[@kuon2008].

@fig-fpga-blocks shows how these blocks are arranged on the chip.

![Simplified structure of an FPGA: logic blocks (LUT and flip-flop), programmable routing, block RAM, a PLL and I/O blocks around the edge. Based on the description in [@kuon2008].](images/ch2_fpga_block_diagram){#fig-fpga-blocks width=80%}

All logic blocks of an FPGA work at the same time. A circuit with four PWM channels
therefore contains four comparators that run in parallel, while a microcontroller would
serve the channels one after another in software. For this thesis, this property is the
main reason to use an FPGA: the node has to receive data, forward data and generate PWM
signals at the same moment.

### Clocking, Timing and Synchronisation {#sec-clocking}

In a *synchronous* design, all flip-flops change their state at the edge of one common
clock. Between two clock edges, each signal has to pass through the logic and the wires
and reach the next flip-flop before the next edge arrives. It must arrive a short time
before the edge (*setup time*) and stay stable for a short time after it (*hold time*).
The slowest path in the design, the *critical path*, sets the highest clock frequency
$f_\text{max}$ at which the design still works. The place-and-route tool calculates this
value after the implementation (@sec-toolchain).

With the clock of this thesis, every path has one clock period to finish:

$$
T_\text{clk} = \frac{1}{f_\text{clk}} = \frac{1}{50\ \text{MHz}} = 20\ \text{ns}
$$ {#eq-clock-period}

The design therefore only works if the $f_\text{max}$ reported by the tool is above
50 MHz. The value reached in this work is given in @sec-hardware.

A special problem arises with signals that come from outside the FPGA, such as the
receive line of a serial interface. Such a signal does not follow the FPGA clock, and its
edges can occur at any time, also inside the setup or hold time of the first flip-flop.
The flip-flop can then become *metastable*: for some time, its output is neither a clean
0 nor a clean 1 [@ginosar2011]. The usual protection is a *two-flip-flop synchronizer*.
The external signal passes through two flip-flops in a row, so a metastable state in the
first flip-flop has one full clock period to settle before the second flip-flop passes the
value on [@ginosar2011].

Ginosar gives the *mean time between failures* (MTBF) of a synchronizer as
[@ginosar2011]:

$$
\text{MTBF} = \frac{e^{S/\tau}}{T_W \cdot f_C \cdot f_D}
$$ {#eq-mtbf}

Here, $S$ is the time the flip-flop has to settle, $\tau$ and $T_W$ are properties of the
flip-flop, $f_C$ is the clock frequency and $f_D$ is the rate at which the input data
changes. Since $S$ stands in the exponent, one extra clock period of settling time raises
the MTBF by a very large factor. This is why a second flip-flop is enough in most designs.

### Microcontroller vs. FPGA vs. ASIC vs. LED Driver IC {#sec-device-comparison}

The tasks of a segment node can be solved with different kinds of devices.
@tbl-device-comparison compares them in general terms.

| **Property**        | **Microcontroller**      | **FPGA**                    | **ASIC**                  | **LED driver IC**             |
|:--------------------|:-------------------------|:----------------------------|:--------------------------|:------------------------------|
| How it works        | software on a processor  | configurable hardware       | fixed custom hardware     | fixed function for LEDs       |
| Parallel tasks      | limited                  | yes                         | yes                       | only its built-in function    |
| Timing              | depends on the software  | exact, clock-based          | exact                     | exact                         |
| Change after design | new software             | new bitstream               | not possible              | not possible                  |
| Development cost    | low                      | medium                      | very high                 | low                           |
| Unit cost           | low                      | medium                      | low only at high volume   | low                           |

: General comparison of device types for a LED node {#tbl-device-comparison}

An FPGA sits between a microcontroller and an ASIC. It has the exact timing and the
parallel operation of hardware, and it can still be changed after the design is
finished. Compared with an ASIC, an FPGA needs more chip area and power for the same
function, because of its programmable structure [@kuon2008]. A common path is therefore to
develop and test a design on an FPGA first and to move it to an ASIC later, when the
number of units is high enough to pay for the ASIC development. The Verilog code in this
thesis is written with this later step in mind (@sec-rtl).

### Cologne Chip GateMate FPGA {#sec-gatemate}

This thesis uses the **GateMate CCGM1A1** from Cologne Chip. The chip is produced by
GlobalFoundries in Dresden, Germany, in a 28 nm process called 28SLP [@eenews_gatemate].
@tbl-gatemate lists its main resources.

| **Resource**                     | **CCGM1A1**                                           |
|:---------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| Programmable elements (CPEs)     | 20,480                                                |
| Flip-flops / latches             | 40,960                                                |
| Block RAM                        | 64 blocks of 20 Kbit or 32 blocks of 40 Kbit          |
| PLLs                             | 4                                                     |
| SerDes                           | 1                                                     |
| GPIOs                            | 162 single-ended or 81 differential (LVDS) pairs      |
| Package                          | 324-ball BGA, 15 × 15 mm                              |

: Main resources of the GateMate CCGM1A1 [@gatemate_summary] {#tbl-gatemate}

The logic block of the GateMate is called *Cologne Programmable Element* (CPE). The CCGM1A1
has 20,480 CPEs, arranged in a matrix of 160 × 128 [@cologne_ds1001]. Each CPE contains a
LUT tree that can be used as two 4-input functions or as one 8-input function, and it can
also work as a 1-bit or 2-bit full adder or as a 2 × 2-bit multiplier. Each CPE has two
outputs, and each output can use its own flip-flop or latch, so the chip has
2 × 20,480 = 40,960 flip-flops or latches [@cologne_ds1001]. The place-and-route tool
nextpnr therefore counts the logic and the flip-flops in half-CPE units, with 40,960
places each (@sec-hw-results).

The core of the chip runs at 0.9 V, 1.0 V or 1.1 V, depending on whether a low-power, an
economy or a speed mode is chosen. The GPIOs work with voltage levels from 1.2 V to 2.5 V
[@cologne_ds1001]. The chip is therefore **not specified for 3.3 V signals**, which has
to be considered when it is connected to other parts such as a USB-to-serial adapter or
an LED driver (@sec-gatemate-board).

Cologne Chip supports the GateMate with an open-source toolchain: Yosys for synthesis,
nextpnr for place and route, and openFPGALoader for programming [@cologne_toolchain].
@sec-toolchain describes these tools.

### GateMate Evaluation Board and Programmer {#sec-gatemate-board}

The hardware tests in this thesis were done on the **GateMate FPGA Evaluation Board**,
versions 3.1 and 3.2 [@gatemate_ds1003]. The board carries the CCGM1A1 and gives access to
108 GPIOs on six 46-pin headers. A 10 MHz oscillator on the board feeds the pin IO_SB_A8,
which is the input for clock 0 of the FPGA. Inside the FPGA, a PLL turns this 10 MHz clock
into the 50 MHz system clock of the design (@sec-clock-reset). Eight user LEDs, D1 to D8,
are connected to GPIO bank EB. The board has its own USB interface (FTDI FT2232H) for
programming over JTAG, so the separate GateMate programmer board was not needed
[@gatemate_ds1003].

The two Pmod connectors of the board are connected to GPIO bank NB through SN74CB3T3245
bus switches with level shifting. Their supply is set to 3.3 V with a jumper to meet the
Pmod specification [@gatemate_ds1003]. The FPGA itself works with I/O levels of at most
2.5 V [@cologne_ds1001], so the outputs on the Pmod pins reach only about 2.5 V. This
level matters for two reasons: the receiving device must accept it as a logic high, and
the driver stage of the LEDs must switch at this voltage (@sec-low-side-switching).

## Digital Design Flow {#sec-design-flow}

The way from a design idea to a programmed FPGA has several steps (@fig-design-flow).
They are explained in the following sections.

![Design flow from the model to the programmed FPGA.](images/ch2_design_flow){#fig-design-flow width=100%}


### HDL and RTL Design with Verilog {#sec-verilog}

Digital hardware is described with a *hardware description language* (HDL). This thesis
uses **Verilog**, which is standardised as IEEE 1364 [@ieee1364]. A Verilog description
consists of *modules* with inputs and outputs, and modules can be connected to build
larger designs.

The design is written at the *register-transfer level* (RTL). At this level, the designer
describes the registers (flip-flops) of the circuit and the logic that computes their next
values at each clock edge. Only a part of the Verilog language can be turned into
hardware; this part is called *synthesizable*. Other constructs, such as delays
(`#10`) or file access, are only used in testbenches.

A design that should later be moved to an ASIC follows a few simple rules: one clock for
the whole design, no device-specific blocks inside the main logic, and clear borders
between modules. Device-specific parts, such as the PLL and the I/O pins, are kept at the
top level of the design (@sec-rtl).

### Simulation and Testbenches {#sec-simulation}

Before a design is loaded onto the FPGA, it is tested in simulation. A *testbench* is a
Verilog module that is not turned into hardware. It creates the input signals, for
example a serial data stream, applies them to the design and checks the outputs. The
results can be printed as text, such as "pass" or "fail", or shown as waveforms. In
simulation, every signal inside the design can be observed, so errors found there are
much easier to locate than errors found on the hardware. In this thesis, the testbench checks the results itself and prints PASS or FAIL
(@sec-rtl-verification).
The simulator used in this thesis is the open-source tool *Icarus Verilog*
[@icarus_verilog]. No waveform viewer was needed, because the testbench compares all
results itself and prints them as text.

### Open-Source Toolchain: Yosys, nextpnr, openFPGALoader {#sec-toolchain}

The implementation of the design on the GateMate uses three open-source tools
[@cologne_toolchain]:

1. *Synthesis with Yosys.* Yosys reads the Verilog code and turns it into a netlist of
   the basic elements of the target FPGA [@shah2019]. For the GateMate, the command
   `synth_gatemate` maps the design onto CPEs, flip-flops and other GateMate elements.
2. *Place and route with nextpnr.* nextpnr places each element of the netlist on a
   position on the chip and connects the elements through the routing network
   [@shah2019]. It also performs a timing analysis and reports $f_\text{max}$ and the
   resource usage.
3. *Programming with openFPGALoader.* openFPGALoader loads the bitstream into the FPGA or
   into its configuration flash memory [@openfpgaloader].

Between place and route and programming, the result is packed into a bitstream file. The
commands used in this thesis are given in @sec-hardware. In Yosys and nextpnr, the
general algorithms are kept apart from the details of each FPGA architecture, so the same
tools can support FPGAs from different vendors [@shah2019].

### Model-Based Design with Simulink {#sec-simulink-basics}

**Simulink** is a graphical environment from MathWorks for modelling and simulating
dynamic systems [@mathworks_simulink]. A model is built from blocks, such as counters,
switches, comparators and memories, which are connected by signal lines. In this thesis,
Simulink is used to model the digital data path before the Verilog code is written. In
this way, the idea of the data path (serial input, latch, parsing and PWM generation) can
be checked at an early stage (@sec-simulink).

## Serial Communication {#sec-serial-communication}

### UART Frame and Sampling {#sec-uart}

A **universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART)** sends data one bit after another
over a single wire. There is no separate clock line. Instead, the sender and the receiver
must be set to the same *baud rate*, the number of bits per second [@adi_uart2020].

When no data is sent, the line stays at a high level. Each data word, called a *frame*,
consists of [@adi_uart2020]:

1. one *start bit*, which pulls the line low and marks the beginning of the frame,
2. the *data bits*,
3. optionally a *parity bit*,
4. one or two *stop bits*, which bring the line back to high.

The data frame can be 5 to 8 bits long when a parity bit is used, and 9 bits long when no
parity bit is used [@adi_uart2020].

@fig-uart-frame shows such a frame with nine data bits, as used by Flexlink.

![UART frame of the 9-bit word 0x176 (EOP) at 1 MBaud, with the sampling point in the middle of each bit.](images/ch2_uart_frame){#fig-uart-frame width=100%}

The duration of one bit is:

$$
T_\text{bit} = \frac{1}{\text{baud rate}}
$$ {#eq-bit-time}

At 1 MBaud, $T_\text{bit} = 1 / 1{,}000{,}000\ \text{s} = 1\ \mu\text{s}$. A frame with 1
start bit, 9 data bits and 1 stop bit has 11 bits and therefore lasts $11\ \mu\text{s}$.

Because there is no clock line, the receiver detects the falling edge of the start bit
and then reads each bit in the middle of its bit time, where the signal is most stable.
In an FPGA, this is done with a counter that runs at the system clock. The number of
clock cycles per bit is:

$$
\text{CLKS\_PER\_BIT} = \frac{f_\text{clk}}{\text{baud rate}}
$$ {#eq-clks-per-bit}

With $50\ \text{MHz} / 1\ \text{MBaud} = 50$ clock cycles per bit, the receiver waits 25
clock cycles after the start edge to reach the middle of the start bit, and then 50 clock
cycles for each further bit.

The sender and the receiver each use their own clock, and the two clocks are never
exactly equal. The small difference adds up over the frame. The frame is still read
correctly as long as the last sample, in the middle of the stop bit, stays inside the
stop bit. For a frame of 11 bits:

1. The middle of the stop bit lies $10.5$ bit times after the start edge.
2. The sample may move by at most half a bit time, $0.5\ T_\text{bit}$, before it leaves
   the stop bit.
3. Allowed total clock difference: $0.5 / 10.5 \approx 4.8\ \%$.
4. If both sides share this equally, each clock may differ by about $\pm 2.4\ \%$.

This estimate does not include the uncertainty of the start-edge detection, which is one
clock cycle, or $1/50$ of a bit at 50 MHz and 1 MBaud.

### 9-bit UART Words {#sec-9bit-uart}

Most UART connections send 8 data bits, but 9 data bits are also possible
[@adi_uart2020]. A common use of the ninth bit is to mark a word as an *address* or
*control* word instead of a normal data byte. Microcontrollers offer this as a
*multi-processor communication mode*: all receivers on the line check the ninth bit and
react only to words in which it is set [@atmega328p].

The Flexlink protocol uses the ninth bit in the same way: it marks the control words that
start and end a packet (@sec-flexlink). A standard PC serial interface does not offer 9
data bits directly. The parity bit can be used as the ninth bit instead: with *mark*
parity the parity bit is always 1, and with *space* parity it is always 0. The Python
library pySerial supports both settings [@pyserial]. This method is used by the PC test
program in this thesis (@sec-hardware).

### Packet Structure and Error Detection {#sec-packets}

Single words are grouped into *packets*. A packet usually has:

- a start marker, so that the receiver knows where the packet begins,
- a command, which says what the packet means,
- the payload, which is the actual data,
- optionally a check value for error detection,
- an end marker.

With a start and an end marker, the receiver can find the borders of a packet again even
after a transmission error. A simple check value is a *checksum*: the sender adds all
data bytes, keeps the lowest 8 bits and sends this value with the packet. The receiver
calculates the same sum and compares it with the received value. A single wrong bit
changes the sum, so the error is detected. A checksum is easy to build in hardware, but
it does not detect every combination of errors, for example two errors that cancel each
other out. *Cyclic redundancy checks* (CRC) detect more errors but need more logic.


### Network Topologies {#sec-topologies}

When many nodes have to receive data from one master, they can be connected in different
ways. @tbl-topologies compares the three basic topologies.

| **Topology**  | **Wiring**                                      | **Delay**                              | **If one node or wire fails**                |
|:--------------|:------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|
| Bus           | one shared line to all nodes                    | the same for all nodes                 | a short circuit can block the whole bus      |
| Star          | one line from the master to each node           | the same for all nodes                 | only that node is lost                       |
| Daisy chain   | each node connects only to its neighbours       | grows with the position in the chain   | all nodes behind the failure are lost        |

: Comparison of network topologies {#tbl-topologies}

In an aircraft cabin, the LEDs are mounted one after another along the cabin. A *daisy
chain* fits this layout, because each segment only needs a short connection to the next
one, and no long lines back to the master are needed. Each node also sends the signal on
with fresh, clean edges. The drawbacks are the growing delay and the fact that a broken
node or wire cuts off all nodes behind it. The delay is treated in the next section.

### Latency in a Daisy Chain {#sec-daisy-latency}

In a daisy chain, every node has to pass on the data for the nodes behind it. There are
two basic ways to do this:

- *Store-and-forward*: the node first receives the complete packet and only then sends
  it on.
- *Cut-through*: the node starts to send the data on as soon as it has received enough
  of it, without waiting for the end of the packet. Kermani and Kleinrock described this
  method as *virtual cut-through* for computer networks [@kermani1979].

The delay per node is very different for the two methods:

$$
t_\text{node,SF} = N_\text{words} \cdot T_\text{word}
\qquad
t_\text{node,CT} \approx T_\text{word}
$$ {#eq-node-delay}

where $N_\text{words}$ is the number of words in the packet and $T_\text{word}$ is the time
for one word. With cut-through, a node can only forward a UART word after it has received
it, which takes about one word time. The exact value for this design is derived in
@sec-rtl.

The total delay up to the last node of a chain with $H$ hops is:

$$
t_\text{total} = t_\text{packet} + H \cdot t_\text{node}
$$ {#eq-total-delay}

The following example shows the size of the effect. It uses a packet of 202 words, an
11-bit word at 1 MBaud ($T_\text{word} = 11\ \mu\text{s}$) and 24 hops:

1. Store-and-forward, per node: $202 \cdot 11\ \mu\text{s} = 2222\ \mu\text{s}$.
2. Store-and-forward, 24 hops: $24 \cdot 2222\ \mu\text{s} \approx 53.3\ \text{ms}$.
3. Cut-through, 24 hops: $24 \cdot 11\ \mu\text{s} = 264\ \mu\text{s}$.

With store-and-forward, the hops alone would take more than 50 ms. With cut-through, they
take about a quarter of a millisecond. The packet size and the time limit of this system
are analysed in @sec-requirements.

This simple example assumes that every node forwards the complete packet. In the design
of this thesis, each node keeps its own eight bytes, so the packet becomes shorter from
node to node. Even then, store-and-forward needs about 29 ms for 25 segments, while
cut-through needs about 2.5 ms (@sec-req-timing).

## The Flexlink Protocol {#sec-flexlink}

**Flexlink** is the serial protocol that AES uses between the master and the led
segments [@aes_flexlink]. It is based on UART words with 9 data bits at 1 MBaud. A ninth bit of 1 marks a *control word*,
and a ninth bit of 0 marks a *data word*. Each packet starts with a control word that
contains the command, the *start of packet* (SOP). Data words follow, and the packet ends
with the *end of packet* word EOP = 0x176.

The direction from the master to the segments is called the **uplink**, and the direction
from the segments back to the master is called the **downlink**. @tbl-flexlink-packets
lists the packet types used in this thesis.

| **Packet**      | **Direction** | **Words**                                                  |
|:----------------|:--------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| LED data        | uplink        | 0x100, then 8 data bytes per node (R, G, B, W, 16 bit each, high byte first), then 0x176 |
| LED answer      | downlink      | 0x180, node ID, temperature, 0x176                         |
| Count segments  | uplink        | 0x160, start ID, 0x176                                     |
| Count answer    | downlink      | 0x1B0, node ID, 0x176                                      |

: Flexlink packets used in this thesis [@aes_flexlink] {#tbl-flexlink-packets}

All command words in @tbl-flexlink-packets, including the end-of-packet word 0x176, are
defined in the Flexlink specification of AES [@aes_flexlink]. This thesis uses them
without changes.

## State of the Art {#sec-state-of-the-art}

In a lighting system with many RGBW segments, every segment needs two functions. It must
**receive** its brightness values over a communication line, and it must **turn these values into PWM signals** for its LEDs. This section describes how these two functions are solved today and which gap this thesis addresses.

### Microcontroller in Every Segment {#sec-sota-mcu}

In the present AES system, every RGBW segment has 8 LEDs in series per colour channel, so
four PWM signals control the light of one segment. The PWM signals are generated by an
**STM32C011F6 microcontroller** in each segment, an Arm Cortex-M0+ processor with up to
48 MHz, two USART interfaces and several 16-bit timers [@st_stm32c011]. One USART
receives the commands from the master and the other passes them on to the next segment,
and the answers of the segments travel back the same way.

Each PWM signal switches an LED driver that sets the current of its channel. AES uses two
types. The BCR421UFD from Diodes is a constant-current regulator for LED strings, whose
current can be set up to 350 mA with an external resistor and whose enable pin accepts a
PWM signal of up to 25 kHz [@diodes_bcr421]. The second type is a transistor circuit
built around the BC846AQB-Q from Nexperia [@nexperia_bc846], in which a Zener diode at
the base and a resistor at the emitter keep the current constant.

This solution is flexible, because the communication is defined in software. Its limits
come from the way a microcontroller works. The program handles the received bytes one
after another, usually started by an interrupt, so the delay of each segment depends on
the software and on what else the processor is doing at that moment
(@sec-device-comparison). For a later integrated circuit, the software would also have to
be rewritten as hardware.

### Addressable LEDs {#sec-sota-addressable}

Addressable LEDs such as the WS2812B show a different way. The control logic and the
LEDs are combined in one small package, and the packages are connected in a chain by a
single data line at 800 kbit/s [@ws2812b]. Each LED takes the first 24 bits of the data
stream, 8 bits for each of the colours green, red and blue, and passes the rest on to the
next LED after reshaping the signal. A pause of more than 50 µs ends the frame
[@ws2812b].

This is the same principle as in a Flexlink chain, *keep your own data and forward the
rest*, but done completely in hardware. The WS2812B shows that this principle needs very
little logic and very little wiring. However, it offers only 8 bits per colour, no white
channel, no answer back to the controller and a fixed protocol that cannot be changed.

### FPGA-Based LED Control {#sec-sota-fpga}

FPGAs are already used to control LEDs, for example to generate PWM signals and to
receive serial commands in an LED dimmer [@avotins2012]. An FPGA works in parallel and is
clocked, so it can generate many PWM channels with exact timing at the same time, and it
can forward serial data with a fixed delay of only a few clock cycles. The method of
forwarding data before the whole packet has arrived, *cut-through*, was first described
for computer networks [@kermani1979]. With the open-source flow of Yosys and nextpnr,
such designs can now also be built for commercial FPGAs without vendor tools
[@shah2019].

### Comparison and Research Gap {#sec-research-gap}

@tbl-state-of-the-art compares the three approaches.

| **Property**                  | **Microcontroller (present AES system)** | **Addressable LED (WS2812B)** | **FPGA node (this thesis)** |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:------------------------------|:----------------------------|
| PWM resolution                | depends on the software and timers       | 8 bit                         | 16 bit                      |
| Forwarding                    | in software                              | in hardware                   | in hardware, cut-through    |
| Delay per segment             | depends on the software                  | fixed                         | fixed, about one word time  |
| Answer to the master          | yes                                      | no                            | yes                         |
| Protocol can be changed       | yes                                      | no                            | yes                         |
| Path to an integrated circuit | software must be rewritten               | —                             | RTL can be reused           |

: Comparison of approaches for controlling RGBW segments {#tbl-state-of-the-art}

The microcontroller supports Flexlink and answers to the master, but its timing depends on
the software. The addressable LED forwards in hardware with a fixed delay, but its
resolution and missing feedback do not meet the needs of a cabin lighting system. In the
sources reviewed for this thesis, no design was found that implements a Flexlink-type
daisy-chain protocol with 16-bit PWM, cut-through forwarding and answers to the master
as **one digital hardware block**, on a European FPGA with an open-source flow, and in a
form that can later be moved to an integrated circuit. This thesis closes this gap with
the Flexlink node described in @sec-rtl. The LED drivers that set the current of each
channel are not part of this replacement and stay as they are.
